newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle may pick up satellite early.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle may pick up satellite early.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Columbia may have to pick up a prototype space factory early, because it was drifting too close to a space telescope, NASA officials said on Sunday.

The Wake Shield Facility, which was set free from Columbia on Friday night, was not due to be recovered until early on Tuesday morning, but the shuttle may have to fly in and collect it early on Monday, mission control told the astronauts.

The saucer-shaped prototype space factory and the Orfeus-Spas telescope, released from Columbia last Tuesday, have unexpectedly drifted together, shuttle flight director Rob Kelso told at news conference.

The two spacecraft must be at least 12.5 miles apart for the shuttle to collect the Wake Shield safely, he said. They were about 25 miles apart on Sunday evening and were getting about 0.8 miles closer with every orbit of earth.
"We may have to call on you guys to roll with it a bit today," spacecraft communicator Bill McArthur said after waking the astronauts at about 2 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Sunday.

"Overnight we've noticed Spas getting just a little bit close to Wake Shield, and I wanted to give you a heads-up that we are looking at the criteria that might require you to go in and do a retrieval at the end of today," McArthur said.
Flight controllers at NASA's mission control in Houston asked military tracking radar to give them a more precise idea of the location of the two satellites.

"We've been spending most of our time ... crunching the computer in the control centre to predict the flight path of the Spas and the Wake shield ... to answer the question who is going to be where when," Kelso said.

The orbiting space factory was designed to use the vacuum of space to manufacture ultra-pure semiconductors for the electronics industry. The semiconductors could lead to faster computer chips and better, smaller cellular phones.
NASA believes the problem arose when the telescope encountered more drag than expected from the thin upper atmosphere 220 miles (355 km) up, causing it to approach the Wake Shield.

For five hours overnight and again on Sunday afternoon, astronomers scaled back their observations with the telescope, so it could be placed in a more aerodynamic position, slowing the rate at which it is closing in on the Wake Shield.
This is the first time NASA has flown the shuttle in formation with two recoverable satellites. Flight director Al Pennington said before the mission that doing so would be "tricky."
The five astronauts, who are one-third of the way through a 16-day mission, took six hours off duty on Sunday. They were expected to make private calls to their families.

If the astronauts are instructed to collect the Wake Shield, it will be plucked from orbit with the Shuttle's robot arm at about 2:45 a.m. EST (0745 GMT) on Monday. The decision whether to collect it will be made around 11 p.m. EST on Sunday (0400 GMT on Monday), Kelso said.
Shuttle commander Ken Cockrell said his crew was prepared to work late to collect the satellite if necessary.
"The crew is ready and willing to stay up almost as late as you'd like to make that happen as late as possible, so that Wake Shield can get some more of its work completed," he told mission control.

One of the seven planned semiconductor manufacturing runs would be abandoned if the satellite had to be collected early, but the project's scientists would still be satisfied, Michael Lembeck, chief engineer for the Wake Shield, said.
"We're just too pleased to be frustrated at this point," he said. "We have achieved our science objectives that we set out for originally. The last growth is what we call an optional growth."
By Sunday evening the space factory had manufactured its fifth semiconductor sample. Controllers planned to make at least one more before the day was out.
